idiom_name: typed memo wrapper: Map<number, ParseResult<T>> per rule with a discriminated union
implementation_notes: The mechanism is JavaScript's - a Map keyed by position plus a wrapper - but the type system changes what should be stored: the memo's value type is a discriminated union ({ ok: true; node: T; next: number } | { ok: false }), so a cached failure is a first-class entry that can never be confused with a missing one, and each rule can be memoized generically (function memoized<T>(impl: (pos: number) => ParseResult<T>)). What replaces the classic structure is that the table and its wrapper are produced per rule by one generic function; has() remains the hit test because Map.get is typed as V | undefined for a missing key regardless of the declared value type. Peggy is the library route: its generated parsers accept --cache to enable exactly this memoization (documented as slower except in pathological cases) and --dts to emit typings for the grammar actions.
pitfalls: Structural typing means every memo is Map<number, ...>: nothing stops a rule from being handed another rule's table - create the cache inside the rule's own closure (as above) or include the rule id in the key.
Map.get is typed V | undefined, so a union result still needs an explicit hit test (has()/!== undefined); with noUncheckedIndexedAccess the same trap appears when an array replaces the Map.
Types are erased: the union prevents mistakes at compile time only, so runtime code (or untyped JavaScript) writing null/undefined into the cache recreates the undefined-vs-missing bug.
